title.text: High Fashion in the Harlem Renaissance

textContent.text: In the 1920s and '30s, a cultural awakening known as the Harlem Renaissance famously transformed African American art, literature, and music. This vibrant movement also revolutionized the world of fashion. New styles demonstrated clothing's power as a form of self-expression and cultural pride celebrating African American identity.

In the early twentieth century, Harlem, a neighborhood in northern Manhattan, became a magnet for African Americans migrating from the South in search of better opportunities. This flow of newcomers turned Harlem into a lively cultural hub, where creativity flourished and fresh ideas took root. Against this backdrop, a new style of dress emerged that would come to define the era.

Before this period, African Americans were often belittled and ridiculed in popular culture for their clothing. Many Black communities were denied access to clothing retailers and tailoring services. Harlem Renaissance fashion aimed to counter stereotypes by favoring dignified, sophisticated looks. Men often sported richly colored, well-tailored suits with crisp white shirts and snazzy fedora hats, presenting an image of genteel refinement. Women embraced the "flapper" style that was popular in U.S. cities, wearing knee-length dresses with silk stockings and bold accessories like long strands of pearls. Designers also included elements of traditional African textiles, like kente cloth's bold, geometric patterns, into the clothing of the era.

Fashion during the Harlem Renaissance was about more than just looking good—it was a form of resistance. Josephine Baker, the celebrated entertainer, proudly illustrated this defiance through her style. Her dazzling attire, including rich, black velvet and glimmering gold dresses, captivated audiences and shattered stereotypes. She became an icon for African American women by projecting an image of grace, wealth, and status.

The era's fashion was also influenced by jazz, the soundtrack of the Harlem Renaissance. The free-spirited nature of the music inspired more liberating clothing styles. Both men's suits and women's dresses became easier to move in, which helped match the pace of the energetic dances popular in Harlem's famous nightclubs. Just as musicians injected their own flair into well-known songs, Black Americans used jewelry and accessories to flaunt their individual styles.

African American designers played a key role in shaping Harlem's fashion scene. Designers like Zelda Wynn Valdes created elegant gowns that celebrated the Black female form. Stars like Ella Fitzgerald radiated confidence and glamor in Valdes's show-stopping designs. Meanwhile, Harlem's residents began organizing their own fashion shows, often featuring affordable handmade clothing that ensured fashion wasn't just for the elite. These shows highlighted the creativity of the local community while also increasing visibility for Black clothing in broader American fashion trends.

The Harlem Renaissance laid the foundation for future expressions of Black pride through clothing. Its influence can be seen in the bold patterns and colors of Civil Rights era fashion, the hip-hop streetwear of the 1980s and '90s, and even in African-inspired designs on modern runways. Since the 1920s, Harlem-born fashions have enriched the cultural and literal fabric of America with their focus on Black beauty, artistry, and joy.

textContent.text: In 1974, a group of farmers in Shaanxi Province, China, made an unexpected discovery while digging a well—they unearthed ancient clay fragments. These fragments drew the attention of curious archaeologists who followed them to a source few could have imagined: an entire army of life-size terra-cotta warriors. These thousands of clay soldiers, horses, and chariots were buried over 2,200 years ago to guard the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, the first Emperor of China. This discovery would prove to highlight the grandeur of Qin Shi Huang's reign and reveal new insights about ancient Chinese culture and craftsmanship.

Qin Shi Huang, born Ying Zheng, ascended to the throne of the Qin state at the age of thirteen. After a series of military conquests, he became the first emperor of a unified China in 221 BCE. A ruthless and driven leader, his policies shaped China for centuries to come. In addition to his work setting standards for the nation's writing system, currency, and measurements, he oversaw massive infrastructure projects like the Great Wall of China. His quest for immortality led him to commission a grand mausoleum guarded by an army of terra-cotta warriors meant to protect him in the afterlife.

The terra-cotta army is a marvel of ancient craftsmanship and engineering. Each warrior is unique, with distinct facial features, expressions, and clothing. The soldiers stand in battle formation, arranged according to rank and duty. The figures were created using assembly line techniques that were advanced for their time. Artisans crafted body parts separately, fired them in kilns, and then assembled and painted the figures. This process, completed with painstaking attention to detail, resulted in a strikingly realistic representation of the emperor's army.

Creating so many intricate statues was an enormous undertaking, involving legions of laborers and artisans. It is estimated that approximately seven hundred thousand workers were involved in the construction of the mausoleum complex, which took around thirty-eight years to complete. This project demonstrated the emperor's immense power as well as the highly organized and skilled workforce of ancient China. The warriors themselves were equipped with real weapons, such as swords, spears, and crossbows. And many of these weapons were coated with chromium to prevent rust, showcasing the advanced technological knowledge of the period.

Qin Shi Huang's tomb complex, which remains largely unexcavated, is believed to contain even more secrets. Ancient texts describe a hidden model of his empire, complete with rivers of highly poisonous mercury guarded by crossbow traps, as well as talismans to protect against spirits in the afterlife. Experts continue to find new statues within the remains of the tomb complex, though some have been damaged during excavation.

Today, the tomb of Qin Shi Huang is a UNESCO World Heritage site that attracts millions of visitors from around the world. The terra-cotta warriors not only showcase the ingenuity and artistry of ancient China but also offer insight into the ambitions and beliefs that shaped this civilization. Qin Shi Huang's immortal defenders remain a powerful reminder of his enduring legacy and humanity's timeless quest to leave a permanent mark on history.

title.text: The Birth of a Business Empire

textContent.text: On March 20, 1602, a groundbreaking business firm emerged that would reshape global commerce. The Dutch East India Company, known as the VOC (Vereenigde Oostindische Compagnie), was the world's first multinational corporation. While often associated with international trade and colonization, the VOC also pioneered business practices that continue to shape corporations in the twenty-first century.

At the dawn of the 1600s, Europe was in the midst of a commercial revolution. Sea trade with Asia offered immense profits but also involved substantial risks. Traditional business models were inadequate for these complex operations. The VOC sought to overcome these challenges by pooling resources, minimizing risks, and designing new ways to manage complex, long-term ventures.

The cornerstone of the VOC's business model was the concept of joint-stock ownership. Unlike earlier companies, where investments were tied to individual voyages, the VOC offered permanent shares representing ownership in the business as a whole. Investors were also free to invest as much or as little money as they chose. This revolutionary approach allowed the company to gather over six million guilders (more than half a trillion modern U.S. dollars) from over one thousand investors, ranging from wealthy merchants to ordinary citizens.

Another key breakthrough of the VOC was the practice of limited liability, a sort of safety net for investors. In the past, if a company failed, investors could lose everything they owned to pay the company's outstanding debts. But with limited liability, investors could only lose the money they put into the company. This made more people willing to invest, dramatically increasing the VOC's investor pool.

To facilitate the buying and selling of shares in the VOC, the company set up the Amsterdam Stock Exchange, which became the world's first stock market. Imagine a market where, instead of fruits and vegetables, people could buy and sell pieces of companies. The value of VOC shares would change based on news from the company's ships returning from far-off lands. The company also invented new ways of trading stocks, like making deals for future trades. These ideas are still used in today's complex financial markets.

The scale of the VOC's operations was unprecedented. By 1669, it commanded well over one hundred merchant ships and forty warships, employed ten thousand soldiers, and had fifty thousand civilians on its payroll. This sprawling global enterprise required new approaches to shipping, communication, and organizational structure. The company developed a detailed system of bookkeeping and correspondence to coordinate its far-flung operations. It also created a new model for managing a large, complex company. Stakeholders elected a group of seventeen leaders called the Heeren XVII (Seventeen Gentlemen). Like a modern board of directors, this group made important choices for the whole organization. The Heeren XVII met regularly and kept investors informed through updates and reports.

Modern corporations still rely on joint-stock ownership and practices like limited liability to raise capital and protect investors. Corporate governance structures, stock markets, and financial instruments all trace their heritage to the VOC's practices. However, there is a darker side to the company's legacy. To secure its profits, the VOC participated in warfare, colonization, and slavery. The company's business practices raised important moral questions that continue to challenge global businesses in our time.

The Dutch East India Company's history can't be separated from its role in colonization and empire. Its influence on the modern business world, however, has been just as lasting. As we navigate the complexities of business and economics today, understanding the origins of these practices provides valuable insight into today's financial systems and their profound impact on society.

At the dawn of the 1600s, Europe was in the midst of a commercial revolution. Sea trade with Asia offered immense profits but also involved substantial risks. Traditional business models were inadequate for these complex operations. The VOC sought to overcome these challenges by pooling resources, minimizing risks, and designing new ways to manage complex, long-term ventures.

The cornerstone of the VOC's business model was the concept of joint-stock ownership. Unlike earlier companies, where investments were tied to individual voyages, the VOC offered permanent shares representing ownership in the business as a whole. Investors were also free to invest as much or as little money as they chose. This revolutionary approach allowed the company to gather over six million guilders (more than half a trillion modern U.S. dollars) from over one thousand investors, ranging from wealthy merchants to ordinary citizens.

Another key breakthrough of the VOC was the practice of limited liability, a sort of safety net for investors. In the past, if a company failed, investors could lose everything they owned to pay the company's outstanding debts. But with limited liability, investors could only lose the money they put into the company. This made more people willing to invest, dramatically increasing the VOC's investor pool.

To facilitate the buying and selling of shares in the VOC, the company set up the Amsterdam Stock Exchange, which became the world's first stock market. Imagine a market where, instead of fruits and vegetables, people could buy and sell pieces of companies. The value of VOC shares would change based on news from the company's ships returning from far-off lands. The company also invented new ways of trading stocks, like making deals for future trades. textContent.text: In the early twentieth century, the natural landscapes that defined the United States were at risk of being lost to rapid industrial growth. President Theodore Roosevelt emerged as a pioneering force for the protection of America's natural treasures. His efforts helped lead to the creation of the National Park System, a protected group of parks, monuments, and historic sites, with the goal of managing wild and beautiful spaces for recreation and wildlife preservation.

Roosevelt was an enthusiastic outdoorsman, hunter, and naturalist. In pursuing these interests, he became deeply moved by the beauty and variety of America's landscapes. Roosevelt's passion for the outdoors became a significant part of his political agenda when he assumed the presidency in 1901.

Roosevelt's key conservation initiatives included new federal institutions and laws to preserve vast areas of land. In 1905, he established the United States Forest Service, which set aside millions of acres as national forests to protect them from unregulated logging, mining, and development. The following year, Roosevelt used the Antiquities Act of 1906 to preserve natural, historical, and cultural landmarks. He named eighteen national monuments during his time in office, including the Grand Canyon and Muir Woods. Roosevelt also helped create five national parks, including Crater Lake and Wind Cave. Distinguished by their unique geographical features, these parks are cherished for their beauty and studied as windows into the distant past.

Roosevelt's efforts resulted in the preservation of over 230 million acres of public land. These protected spaces provided safe habitats for countless species of plants and animals, including some on the brink of extinction. The parks also promoted opportunities for recreation, education, and public health through outdoor activities. Moreover, they became significant drivers of tourism, attracting millions of visitors annually.

Roosevelt's vision and action laid the foundation for the National Park System as a whole. The National Park Service, created to manage these sites, was officially established in 1916, seven years after Roosevelt left office. Of the thirty-five sites the Park Service oversaw in its first year, Roosevelt helped create twenty-three.

But the large-scale benefits of Roosevelt's policies came at serious and lasting costs. Many of the lands named as national parks and monuments were historically inhabited by Indigenous communities, some of whom had lived on the land for thousands of years. These native communities had long practiced sustainable land management and conservation. However, the establishment of national parks often led to conflicts over land use and ultimately to the expulsion of entire Indigenous populations. In the late twentieth century, the National Park Service began to recognize the damage that this displacement had caused to both the disrupted ecosystems and the Indigenous peoples who once cared for them.

Since Roosevelt's presidency, the National Park System has grown into a vast network of protected areas. From the towering peaks of the Rocky Mountains to the serene beauty of the Everglades, national parks cover varied landscapes and ecosystems across the country. Roosevelt's work has also had a global influence, inspiring the creation of national parks and protected areas around the world.

Through his leadership and vision, Roosevelt created a model for environmental stewardship that remains important today. His work demonstrates the critical roles that political action and public support play in the preservation of natural wonders for future generations to enjoy.

content.text: paragraphs 7 and 9

textContent.text: Before the invention of the printing press, sharing knowledge was a slow and painstaking process. Scholars and scientists relied on hand-copied manuscripts, which were rare, expensive, and often filled with errors. This meant that scientific knowledge was limited to a privileged few, and new discoveries spread slowly, if at all.

In the year 1440, Johannes Gutenberg's printing press changed everything. This revolutionary machine used movable metal type, allowing books to be produced quickly and in large numbers. Within fifty years, there were over one thousand printing shops in Europe, producing an estimated eight million books—more than all European scribes had produced in the previous thousand years combined.

This resulted in a profound impact on scientific communication. Printed books made scientific knowledge more accessible and affordable. Scientists could now share their ideas and discoveries with a much wider audience. Importantly, the printing press allowed for the standardization of scientific language and diagrams. Before, hand-drawn illustrations might vary from copy to copy, but printed images ensured everyone was literally on the same page.

Consider the story of Nicolaus Copernicus. In 1543, Copernicus published his groundbreaking theory that the Earth revolves around the Sun, not the other way around. This historic work was based on Copernicus's own astronomical measurements as well as those captured by others in printed texts, a wealth of knowledge that made the Copernican model of the solar system possible. Once printed, his own ideas spread quickly, challenging common knowledge. Within a few decades, copies of his book had reached scientists across Europe, inciting debate and further research.

The printing press also amplified voices that might otherwise have been lost to history. Take Maria Sibylla Merian, a seventeenth-century female naturalist and scientific illustrator. Her detailed drawings of insects and plants, published in several books, reached a wide audience thanks to the printing press. Her work contributed significantly to the field of entomology, the study of insects. Without the printing press, her groundbreaking observations might have remained unknown.

As information spread faster, scientific progress accelerated. Scientists could build on each other's work more quickly, leading to what we now call the Scientific Revolution. The printing press also gave rise to scientific journals, allowing researchers to share their findings more efficiently. This practice evolved into the peer-review process we now use today, in which experts evaluate new research before it's published.

However, the printing press had unintended consequences, too. Just as it could spread accurate information, it could also spread misinformation. False ideas or poorly conducted research could reach a wide audience just as easily as good science. What's worse, scientists also had to contend with disinformation—lies deliberately spread to undermine others' findings or profit off of people's trust in experts.

The legacy of the printing press in scientific communication is immense. It expanded access to knowledge, accelerated the pace of new discoveries, and laid the groundwork for modern scientific collaboration. In many ways, the internet revolution of our time mirrors the printing revolution of the fifteenth century. Both have dramatically changed how we share and consume information.

As you browse websites or scroll through social media feeds, consider the scientists five hundred years ago, excitedly poring over newly printed books. Like them, we have a world of knowledge at our fingertips. And like them, we face the challenge of separating fact from fiction in a sea of information. Nevertheless, the early successes of the printing press remind us that sharing ideas responsibly can change the world for the better.

header.text: A direct object is the pronoun, noun, or noun phrase that receives the action of a verb. To find the direct object in a sentence, locate the action verb and ask "what" or "whom" it is acting on.

sentences.text: Jane admires her neighbor.
Whom does Jane admire? her neighbor
Her neighbor is the direct object in the sentence.
Charlie baked a cake.
What did Charlie bake? a cake
A cake is the direct object in the sentence.

header.text: Some verbs that have a direct object can also have an indirect object. An indirect object is the pronoun, noun, or noun phrase that receives the direct object of a verb. The indirect object always appears in between a verb and its direct object. To find the indirect object in a sentence, locate the action verb and its direct object and ask "to what" or "to whom" the direct object is being given or "for what" or "for whom" the action is being performed.

sentences.text: Charlie baked his mom a cake.
For whom did Charlie bake a cake? for his mom
His mom is the indirect object in the sentence.

header.text: Be careful not to confuse an indirect object with an object of a preposition. An object of a preposition is a pronoun, noun, or noun phrase that comes directly after a preposition, such as to, for, in, under, or during.

sentences.text: Charlie baked a cake for his mom.

Here, his mom is an object of a preposition, not an indirect object. You can tell because his mom comes directly after the preposition for, and because it does not appear in between the verb baked and the direct object a cake.
